claims.text: Reactive molecular dynamics simulations can guide the optimization of dealloying parameters for NM-HEA precursors.
Simulation-guided dealloying will enable controlled synthesis of NM-HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Simulation-guided dealloying will produce nanoframeworks with enhanced surface area.
Simulation-guided dealloying will improve atomic ordering in the resulting nanoframeworks.
The starting materials are multi-element NM-HEA alloy precursors prepared by conventional synthesis.
Chemical or electrochemical dealloying can be conducted using parameters refined by reactive molecular dynamics simulations.
A controlled dealloying environment at ambient or moderately elevated temperature facilitates selective elemental dissolution.
Selective leaching during dealloying mediates self-assembly into three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Atomistic simulations can elucidate interatomic interactions in NM-HEA precursors.
Atomistic simulations can elucidate phase stability in NM-HEA precursors.
Knowledge of interatomic interactions and phase stability permits precise tuning of dealloying conditions.
Optimized dealloying parameters facilitate controlled dissolution of selected elements.
Controlled selective dissolution produces a nanoframework with a tailored atomic structure and high surface area.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframeworks will have a more uniform and catalytically active atomic arrangement than conventionally produced materials.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframeworks will exhibit enhanced catalytic performance relative to conventionally produced materials.
Conventional high-temperature solid-solution synthesis or dealloying without simulation guidance typically produces less-controlled nanoarchitectures.
Scale-up may limit the success of simulation-optimized dealloying parameters.
Differences between simulations and experimental conditions may limit transferability of the optimized parameters.
